title: About Chat
description: Chat is >x<'s encrypted direct messaging feature, using end-to-end encryption to keep messages secure. Learn who can use it, how to send messages, and about message request limits.

runs: How does it work?

>x< and the >x< Chat app (more details below and throughout) includes a new Direct Messaging feature (“Chat”). When entering Chat for the first time, a private-public key pair is created specific to each user. Users are prompted to enter a PIN (which never leaves the device), which is used to keep the private key securely stored on >x<’s infrastructure. This private key can then be recovered from any device if the user knows that PIN. In addition to the private-public key pairs, there is a per-conversation key that is used to encrypt the content of the messages. The private-public key pairs are used to exchange the conversation key securely between participating users.

We employ a combination of strong cryptographic schemes to encrypt every single message, link, and reaction that are part of an encrypted conversation before they leave the sender’s device and remain encrypted while stored on >x<’s infrastructure. Once messages are received by the recipient devices, they are decrypted so that they can be read by the user.
Who is eligible for Chat?
Users need to satisfy the following conditions in order to send and receive encrypted Chat messages:
Both sender and recipient have registered for Chat on (1) the >x< iOS or Android apps or on web or (2) has downloaded the >x< Chat app and signed in using >x< login credentials; and
Recipient
follows or subscribes to the sender, has sent a message to sender previously, or has accepted an encrypted Chat message from the sender before; or
is a member of the same
or
as sender.
Sending Chat message requests
Users may be able to send an unencrypted message request to another user that they do not follow if such other user:
Has opted to receive Chat messages from anyone; or
Is Verified and has opted in to receive Chat messages from other Verified users (and the sender is a Verified user).

If you send a message request to another user, these requests are kept separate from other Chat messages until accepted, similar to legacy DMs. A recipient user can accept the request to continue the conversation, ignore the conversation, or block the sending user. Message requests are unencrypted until the user accepts the request, at which point both users will be informed when the conversation becomes encrypted. Grok is used to help classify these message requests into the ‘Priority’ or ‘Hidden’ message requests inboxes.
Message request limits
Based on your subscription tier, you are limited in the number of message requests you can send in a 24-hour period. The current limits are as follows:
Premium Business: 500
Premium Plus: 75
Premium: 35
Free: 7
If you would like to unlock more message requests, click
to upgrade your subscription tier.
>x< Numbers

An >x< Number is a private code you can create and share so people can message or call you on Chat even if you do not follow them. Having an >x< Number is optional, but does not affect what other people see when they try to message you. It is an extra way for people to reach you. It is not required for people to send you a message request if your inbox already accepts them.
Your >x< Number is not a phone number. It is also not the same as a Chat safety number (see below). Only share your >x< Number with people you want to be able to contact you.
What an >x< Number does
If you enable an >x< Number and someone enters it:
They can message you even if you do not follow them and even if you have a closed inbox.
The conversation goes to your inbox, not message requests.
They can also call you, subject to your
If you have a closed inbox, people you do not follow cannot message you unless they enter your >x< Number, and only if your >x< Number is enabled.

People with whom you have already exchanged messages with in a direct conversation can see your >x< Number. They may share it with others. Anyone who has the current number can use it to message or call you while it is enabled, even if you do not follow them. You can hide your number from other people by turning on the “Hide from others” setting in the >x< Number sheet.
People you follow, people you already have a Chat with, and members of the same
or
can still reach you without an >x< Number.
If you see a prompt asking for someone’s >x< Number
This prompt does not mean you must have their >x< Number to contact them.
If their inbox accepts message requests, you can send a message without an >x< Number. Your message goes to their message requests. You will not see an >x< Number prompt here.

If they have a closed inbox, you will see that they have a closed inbox, and you will be asked for their >x< Number. You cannot send a message unless they follow you, you already have a Chat with them, or you enter their enabled >x< Number.
You may see the >x< Number prompt even if the other person has not created an >x< Number, or has turned theirs off. This is expected. We do not reveal whether someone has an >x< Number.
A Message button may appear on a profile even if that account has a closed inbox. Opening the conversation does not mean you can message them without meeting one of the conditions above.
How to create, share, turn off, or refresh your >x< Number
Open Chat.
Enter your Chat PIN if asked.
Open the inbox dropdown menu.
Tap on "Number".
From there you can:
Turn Enabled on to start using an >x< Number, or off to stop using it.
Tap Share to send your number to people you want to hear from.
Tap Refresh to replace your number with a new one. People who only have the old number will not be able to use it to reach you as a new contact.

Only share your >x< Number with people you want contacting you. If it is shared more widely than you intended, turn it off or refresh it. You will know if someone has contacted you by using your >x< Number, and can refresh it immediately.

Turning off or refreshing your >x< Number does not remove the >x< Number prompt other people may see when they try to message you. It only controls whether entering a number will actually reach your inbox.
How to send an encrypted Chat message?
Tap the compose message button and search for a recipient. Compose a message and click send.

If the user you are messaging has not registered for Chat, they will not have a public key, so the message will be sent unencrypted. When creating a new >x< Chat conversation, this will be communicated by an unlock icon next to the send button.
Registration / Unregistration

Users can register for Chat by entering the Chat tab in the toolbar or downloading the >x< Chat app and signing into an existing >x< account, and following the instructions. This will initiate the creation of a public-private key pair which can then be retrieved from any device. To remove your private key from a device, log out of the account.
Limitations
At this time, only existing >x< accounts can sign into the >x< Chat app. In order to create an >x< account, download the >x< iOS or Android app or visit
on web and follow the instructions (additional information can be found
We welcome feedback and are actively working on improving every aspect of the product, from user experience to protocol security.
Unlike before, group messages and media can now be encrypted.
Content

The contents of an encrypted Chat conversation are encrypted, including any links, media, or files. Reactions to messages are also encrypted. This is not the case while Grok is in the Chat. It is important to note that while the message content itself is encrypted, associated metadata (e.g., recipient, creation time, etc.) is not. If Posts are shared in an encrypted Chat, >x< will have a record that those Posts were shared.
New devices
There is no limit to the number of devices that can use Chat on >x<.
Safety numbers
Safety numbers are a way for you to verify your Chat is with who you think it is. Compare safety numbers with anyone you have a Chat with. They should match!

On the technical side, the safety number is derived with the public key from both people in the Chat. Every message is signed with the other person's public key, meaning that if the safety numbers match, the messages could not have come from anyone else.
Reporting

Message reporting has been built and added as a feature. Upon long-clicking on a message, you have the option to report a message that you believe is in violation of one of >x<’s policies. This reporting function will send that message, its contents, and associated metadata to allow our agents to conduct a review and potentially action against the sending user. In order to verify that the reported message was indeed sent through the Chat system, a cryptographic technique, also known as message franking, will be employed to make that determination. about an account itself and our team will take a look.

Logout and key backup

If at any time you log out from >x<, all messages including encrypted Chat messages on your current device will be deleted; this will not impact any other devices on which you are logged in. Note that if you are signed into both the >x< app and the >x< Chat app, you must sign out of both apps for the messages on your device to be deleted.

Upon logging out, >x< will erase any private keys and conversation keys, unless you have used the device-managed passcode option - in which case the passcode is stored on your iCloud Keychain (for iOS devices only). If you log back in on the same device, your device will be able to re-fetch and decrypt the encrypted conversations using the private key that the device had access to before logging out.

If you cannot remember your PIN, you can change it from a mobile device where you already use Chat. If you do not have one, you can reset your PIN, but you will lose access to your encrypted chat history. Learn how in

runs: Forward secrecy

If the private key of a registered device is compromised, an attacker would be able to decrypt all encrypted Chat messages that were sent and received by that device. In other words, this implementation is not “forward secure.” We are working on mechanisms to allow private key rotation to offer some forward security in the future.
How to change or reset your Chat PIN

Your Chat PIN is the 4-digit code you created when you first entered Chat. In the app, it is called your passcode. Chat asks for it when you use a new device so it can recover your encryption keys and decrypt your previous messages.
Your PIN never leaves your device, so >x< cannot look it up or recover it for you. If you forget it, you have two options:
from a mobile device where you already use Chat. You keep your encrypted chat history.
You lose access to your encrypted chat history. Your unencrypted messages are not affected.
Change your PIN on a mobile device where you use Chat
Use a mobile device where you are signed in to the >x< app and Chat is synced. This is usually the device you used to create your PIN.
Go to your Chat inbox.
Tap the gear icon.
Scroll down and tap "Change passcode".
Enter your new passcode and confirm it.
If Chat asks for your PIN on another device
Select "Forgot passcode".
Select "Change passcode". >x< sends a notification to your mobile device that says "Chat passcode reset".
On your mobile device, tap the notification. Then enter your new passcode and confirm it.
On the device that asked for your PIN, select "Enter new passcode" and enter your new PIN.
If you cannot change your PIN
If you do not have a mobile device where you use Chat, you can reset your PIN. When you reset your PIN, you lose access to your encrypted chat history. Your unencrypted messages are not affected.
When Chat asks for your passcode, select "Forgot passcode".
Select "Change passcode".
Select "Can't change passcode?"
Select "Yes, reset passcode".
Follow the prompts to create a new PIN.

Do not keep guessing if you are unsure of your PIN. After 20 incorrect attempts, your encrypted chat history becomes permanently inaccessible, even if you remember your PIN later. Store your PIN in a password manager, and stay signed in to Chat on at least one mobile device so you can change your PIN if you forget it.
Encrypted message deletion

Chat allows users to “unsend” a message, which will remove it from the recipient’s inbox. This is only possible for encrypted messages. Deleting or leaving an encrypted conversation will not prevent the other person from sending you a DM (encrypted or not) in the future.

When you delete an encrypted message or conversation (sent or received), the data will be instantly deleted from your device (and soon after, from all your other devices). You will no longer be able to view it. Note that the recipient may still be able to see the encrypted message or conversation you have deleted.
Disappearing encrypted messages

Chat offers a new feature called disappearing messages, which allows a user to select a duration, after which messages will be deleted from the device and >x<’s servers. To set the duration, navigate to the conversation info screen and tap the “Disappearing messages” menu.
Edit with Grok / Ask Grok / @Grok

You can edit an image with Grok or ask Grok to analyze your message. Select the image or message and pull up the context menu. Select ‘Ask Grok’ to open the selected image or message in the Grok tab. Note that once you send to Grok, that image or text is no longer encrypted (the contents within the original conversation are still encrypted).

Premium Plus users can add @Grok as a member of any X Chat conversation. This allows interactions with @Grok within the chat. If you add @Grok as a member of a Chat conversation, X and SpaceXAI (to provide the feature) will get access to all the messages in that conversation, from the moment Grok is added until the moment Grok is removed.
You can read more about Grok
Additional note-worthy features

Easily create a group conversation by creating a public link and sharing it directly with other users or to your Timeline. Users who click the link and request to join will only be added if you approve them, and admin(s) can enable and disable the Group Chat invite link at any time. Custom avatars and the Group Chat name will be unencrypted and publicly available.

Record a voice note by selecting the audio icon in the right of the text box. Once recorded, select the stop button. Users are able to listen to the voice note prior to sending it in the conversation.
Where are my private keys stored?

End-to-end encrypted Chats on >x< require each user to have a private-public key pair. This key pair helps securely exchange conversation secrets that encrypt your messages from sender to recipient. A primary challenge with end-to-end encryption is safely storing the private key - access to it would allow someone to read your messages.
Many apps store private keys only on your device, but this can make it difficult to access your Chats seamlessly across multiple devices, which isn't the experience most >x< users expect.

To address this, >x< uses the open-source Juicebox protocol to securely store your private key in the cloud while keeping it protected. The Juicebox protocol splits your secret key into multiple shares, which are stored across independent servers (called "realms"). Your key can only be recovered using the PIN you set when enabling encrypted Chats - this PIN never leaves your device.
In >x<'s implementation:
Your key shares are stored across three Juicebox realms, all currently operated by >x<.
Two of these are hardware-backed realms that use Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) to encrypt your data before it's stored.
Recovering your key requires at least two of the three shares, ensuring that at least one always comes from a hardware-backed realm for added security.
We've published details about the key setup ceremony for these hardware realms here:
Can >x< access my Chats by guessing my PIN?
No. The Juicebox protocol is designed to prevent brute-force attacks, even if someone controls all the realms.

Hardware-backed realms include a built-in guess counter with a strict limit. For Chats, this limit is set to 20 incorrect attempts. After the limit is reached, the key shares become permanently inaccessible. This protection is cryptographically enforced using a Merkle tree structure, where the root is securely stored in the HSM's protected enclave. The software running on the HSMs is open sourced here:
This means that even >x< cannot guess or brute-force your PIN to recover your private key and access your Chats.
In the future, we plan to give users more options, such as choosing realms operated by different organizations to further distribute trust and self-custody of keys.
